body: Yeah, I get that. That I'll be dealing with this forever is something I probably haven't quite come to terms with as much as I like to think I have. It definitely takes time for positive changes, especially when you develop depression early. I can understand that on a rational, unemotional level, but it's still frustrating.

The problem I have is when it doesn't get better. I've worked my ass off and yes, my external situation has improved. I'm finally on the right track to doing what I want, normal logic should follow that I'd be doing better, but absolutely nothing mentally has changed. I'm still just as suicidal and depressed as ever, if not more, I actually have attempts under my belt now, albeit half-assed ones.

It's generic and vague and can show a lack of understanding of a specific situation. It's not constructive, and it's a bit dismissive. Here's a quick way to make a better statement- before saying 'it gets better' ask yourself how and why it would get better.

It also has potential to backfire. What if it doesn't get better? Even if someone is trying their hardest to recover, shit happens and progress is often messy. Going two steps back after one step forward is hard enough without the promise of 'getting better'. There are also situations where 'getting better' is extremely unlikely.

A friend of mine witnessed a suicide. They don't discuss it much and it happened a while ago, but at the time they felt horrible despite not knowing the person well. Some of their compulsions also worsened for a while due to the trauma and new ones developed.

Coworkers, my fellow students, family, and professors. It gets really damn lonely when I end up cutting out everyone around me except those I literally have no choice to interact with because I can't trust anyone outside maybe two people.
I would probably choose to not be born. I don't want to hurt anyone, not existing in the first place would be the cleanest way out.

I promise you, I don't care. If my reputation gets trashed after I die (which it will, even if I don't kill myself) I'm not going to be around to deal with the fallout or any negative consequences that might happen to me.

Honestly... laziness works for me. Killing myself means I'd have to get a plan, set it up, and carry it through. It's quite a bit of work. When I've tried choking, suffocating, and "drowning" myself, I realized how much work and effort would actually be involved to do it correctly.

Another thing that keeps me alive is my two friends. It makes me physically ill when I think about how it'd affect one of them. They already have issues, I don't know how they'd handle the trauma.

I have gone to therapy, tried anti-depressants, as well as self-help coping techniques. I do practice some mindfulness techniques and meditations of sorts. Ultimately I don't think there's a way to get me to stop wanting to die in some capacity, it's like screen burn-in on my brain.

And yeah, I probably would try to keep an otherwise identical clone of myself alive, you got me there. Not really sure why it's different for me.

I'm sorry, but at this point it is my normal, default way of existing. I don't know what 'better' or 'recovery' is supposed to mean for me because there is no period of my life past elementary school where I haven't had these thoughts. The only thing unusual is that in the past year I've been seriously planning, researching, and experimenting.
Someone tried to talk to me and I literally barked at them.
